title: Why El Vicario tastes the way it does

lede.text: A river and a reservoir soften the weather around these vines, and the shallow ground is rich in calcium. The wines that come from it are fine and balanced, with a faint note of scrub.

chapters.title: A strip beside the Guadiana
paras: El Vicario is a place beside the River Guadiana, named after the El Vicario dam. The zone reaches about 2 km from the riverbed and runs for 7 km. It lies entirely in the municipality of Ciudad Real and covers 1,252 hectares.
The land rolls gently and generally falls towards the river. Around the vines grows low holm oak woodland with shrubs.
The zone is surrounded by DOP La Mancha, but its conditions are substantially different. It was drawn around its calcium-rich limy soil and the influence of the river.

fly.label: El Vicario dam on the Guadiana
fly.caption: The zone takes its name from the El Vicario dam and follows the river, about 2 km wide and 7 km long.

chapters.title: A river that calms the weather
paras: The river and the nearby reservoir give the area a milder mesoclima, a local climate of its own. It limits extreme weather.
That gentler climate softens ripening. It helps give the wines fine aromas, with a feel of low scrub.

chapters.title: Shallow, limy ground
paras: The soil is limy and light in texture. It is shallow and well drained, with medium fertility.
Calcium averages over 15 meq/100 g (over 3,000 ppm). Other vineyard soils in Castilla-La Mancha average 8-10 meq/100 g (1,600-2,000 ppm).

Calcium plays a key part in the quality of grape skins. The skins help form the polyphenols and aroma compounds. The wines have a relatively high pH, yet they taste fresh because the tannins are fine.

chapters.title: Whites from red grapes, and a sweet red
paras: Two white grapes are allowed: Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc. Seven red grapes are allowed. The native ones are Tempranillo, Garnacha tinta and Graciano. The foreign ones are Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Petit Verdot.
The rules cover white, white from red grapes, rosado (rosé) and red. The white can be dry or semi-sweet, and one red is sweet.

The dry white is Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, fermented partly in barrel. At least 15% of the must ferments in oak and stays there 4 to 8 months. A smaller share of Garnacha tinta or Tempranillo, made without maceration, may join it.
The white from red grapes is made in steel tanks at 11 to 20 °C. It ranges from steely yellow to pale pink, and against the light a pink tone may show.
The rosado is made from Petit Verdot. It has balsamic notes of eucalyptus and hints of aniseed.
The semi-sweet white is Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc. Its fermentation is stopped by chilling, with 12 to 45 g/l of sugar left.
The reds blend native grapes with foreign ones, or use native grapes only. At least 30% of the wine spends 3 months or more in oak. The rest stays in tank for freshness.
The sweet red is pure Merlot, picked at over 280 g/l of sugar. Its fermentation is stopped by chilling, with 46 to 90 g/l of sugar left. Neither sweet wine is fortified.
Pressing may not go above 2 bar. It may yield at most 70 litres for every 100 kg of grapes.
